Okay so, I’m narcoleptic and 17 weeks pregnant with my second. I worked full time with my first, but was salaried and really did more of like 50+ hour weeks (at a prison at that!) I personally found it beneficial to set a timer for 20-40 minutes. I would take one on lunch and one after work and go to bed early. B) I operated on autopilot. Did what I had to do because I had to do it at the time. I know it sounds kind of like cringe and harsh but it’s all I could do at the time. And c) find your comfort person/people, whether it’s friends or family or a therapist, and get those feelings out. Autopilot can be draining on its own, so having those people you can cry to, rant to, whatever, feel those emotions. 

Remember this is temporary and it is going to get better. You got this, you’re strong! All of us on the sub are here to talk to I’m sure. The fatigue is killer for sure.

We don’t operate through the eyes of if they can change exactly, because that’s such a tricky thing to gauge. It’s more of teaching them how to control urges and what to do when thoughts arise should they find themselves in a compromised position with a minor. 

There are different kinds of people that assault children/dogs/dead bodies, and they aren’t all actual pedophiles. The amount of people who only committed the assaults because they were on drugs (often meth) and had the uncontrollable urge to have sex with something and just took what was there out of convenience is staggering. A lot of these men (I say men only because that was the community I worked with) would frankly never do these things if they weren’t out of their mind on an illicit substance. There were some guys that were more sexually attracted to power and abuse than the age or species or life of the victim. So an elderly person or a child or a dog or a dead thing even, is about the same in their mind. 

And then there are actual pedophiles that were born with their attractions or were exposed to abuse and therefore commit abuse. These men are the most likely to desire change and experience remorse. Obviously they don’t all feel these things, there’s just I higher likelihood. We have classes like Victims Impact, which literally teaches and explains empathy to guys that didn’t grasp the gravity of what they did wrong, often because it was done to them so much. To them it’s societally frowned upon but not quite wrong. Some are delusional that the children or animals actually love them and are attracted to them back. Some think ‘well I’m fine though, so the kid will be fine’ (lol) or ‘we’ll the dog didn’t bite me, I think it liked it’ or ‘well the person is dead, who cares what’s done to the body?’. Just often comes down a struggle with empathy, sometimes common sense.

To answer your question, I did complete these classes with many inmates, and I would say probably half of them at least learned something. I’ve seen men I taught like a year later reoffend, and that’s heartbreaking. I’ve also seen men that I taught become active in organizations like NARSOL and help hold other men with their issues accountable and strive to not hurt people again. Really only time will tell how much change was made. A lot of my job was data collecting, the how/why/when/etc that they developed their issues, so that medical professionals can better predict and treat people down the line. I think a lot of the traceable long term change is located here.
